{{Short description|Marine biologist}}

[[File:Steve Palumbi on Climate Change Recovery (52391781204).jpg|thumb|right|Palumbi in 2022]]
'''Stephen R. Palumbi''' (born October 17, 1956)<ref name = CV /> is an American zoologist who is the Jane and Marshall Steel Jr. Professor in [[Marine Science]]s at [[Stanford University]]<ref name = Stanford-Bio /> at [[Hopkins Marine Station]].<ref name = Stanford-Coral /><ref name = Woods-Bio />  He also holds a Senior Fellowship at the [[Stanford Woods Institute for the Environment]].<ref name = Hopkins-Bio />

== Early life ==
Palumbi was born in [[Baltimore, MD|Baltimore, Maryland]]. He received his [[Bachelor of Arts|B.A.]] in [[biology]] from the [[Johns Hopkins University]] in 1978 and his [[PhD|Ph.D.]] in [[zoology]] from the [[University of Washington]] in [[marine ecology]] in 1984.<ref name = CV /><ref name = Stanford-Bio />  He received the Buell Award from the [[Ecological Society of America]] in 1984.<ref name = CV />

== Career ==
From 1985 to 1996, he worked in the Department of Zoology at the [[University of Hawaii]], winning the Matsuda Fellowship Award for Faculty Research in 1991 and a University of Hawaii Regents Medal for Excellence in Research in 1996.<ref name = CV />  He was promoted to [[Professor|full professor]] in 1994 and appointed the director of the Kewalo Marine Laboratory in 1995.<ref name = CV />  Palumbi moved to a professorship at [[Harvard University]] in 1996 and on to [[Stanford University]] in August 2002.<ref name = Woods-Bio />  In 2007, he was appointed the Harold A. Miller Director of the [[Hopkins Marine Station]], and was appointed to the Jane and Marshall Steel Chair of Biology in 2009.<ref name = CV />

In 1996, Palumbi was awarded a Pew Fellowship in Marine Conservation, which he used "to develop more rapid, cost-efficient, nonradioactive genetic test procedures to identify threatened species of cetaceans found in products taken from whale meat markets ... allow[ing] the focus of management efforts to be the individual, rather than the species or stock, and enables the tracing of particular whales from fishery to market."<ref name = Pew />

In 2003, he was elected a Fellow of the [[California Academy of Sciences]]<ref name = CV /><ref name = FCAS /> and was awarded the [[Peter Benchley Ocean Awards|Peter Benchley Ocean Award for Excellence in Science]] in 2011.<ref name = PBA-About /><ref name = PBA-List />

=== Research interests ===
Palumbi's research interests include studying evolution and change using [[molecular genetics]] techniques, marine [[population biology]] and [[Marine conservation|conservation]], and the effects of human activity on ocean systems.<ref name = Stanford-Bio /> Some of his well known work includes research on using genomic methods to identify species resilient to climate change, and using genetic approaches to identify species of conservation concern in wildlife markets.

== Public engagement ==
In 2003, Palumbi participated in the documentary TV series ''[[The Future Is Wild]]'',<ref name = Stanford-Bio /> appearing in his capacity as [[Harvard University]] Professor of Marine Sciences in the initial episode, [[Welcome to the Future (The Future Is Wild episode)|Welcome to the Future]], as well as in four other episodes where he was also credited as a principal scientific advisor: [[Waterland (The Future is Wild episode)|Waterland]], [[Flooded World]], [[The Endless Desert]], and [[The Global Ocean]]. The series explored possible evolutionary changes in the future over the period of five to two hundred million years, and was developed over a period of four years by a team of scientists whose work was visualised through [[computer animation]].<ref name = TFiW-Independent /><ref name = TFiW-Webpage />

=== Publications ===
Palumbi has written several books:
*The Evolution Explosion: How Humans Cause Rapid Evolutionary Change, 2002.<ref name = Book2002 />
*The Death and Life of Monterey Bay: A Story of Revival, 2011 (with Carolyn Sotka).<ref name = Book2011 /> 
*The Extreme Life of the Sea, 2014 (with Anthony R. Palumbi).<ref name = Book2014 />
He has also been an author of more than 200 scientific papers.<ref name = Palumbi-Pubs />

== Personal life ==
Palumbi is married to a [[physician]], Mary Roberts, and is the father to two grown children.  His interests include music, and was part of the group who founded the band ''Sustainable Sole''.<ref name = Stanford-Bio />

While Palumbi was at Harvard, [[Jonathan Wells (intelligent design advocate)|Jonathan Wells]] hit a [[home run]] off of Palumbi while he was [[pitch (baseball)|pitching]] in a pick-up game.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://arn.org/docs/pjweekly/pj_weekly_011202.htm|title=The Weekly Edge Update: Wells Hits a Home Run at Harvard|date=2001-12-02|first=Phillip E.|last=Johnson|website=[[Access Research Network]]}}</ref>
